To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) a constant-age population of galaxies with cycling or fading star formation rates does not provide an adequate explanation of the excess number of faint blue galaxies, (2) a population of galaxies with constant star formation rates, as postulated in the Gronwall and Koo model, can provide a satisfactory explanation of the excess if the star formation rate is sufficiently low, (3) the excess number of very blue galaxies is consistent with the hypothesis that they are galaxies with star formation rates that are declining with

the deep galaxy counts cannot be reproduced by a model of constant star formation rate and that the deep galaxy number counts cannot be produced by a population of galaxies that fade after a fixed time interval.

(1) the excess of very faint, blue galaxies in the galaxy counts cannot be explained by a population of galaxies with a constant star formation rate, because the implied excess of low-redshift, blue galaxies in other surveys is too high and (2) the excess of faint, blue galaxies can only be explained by a model in which the star formation rates of the galaxies are cycling, because the implied number of faint, red galaxies is too high in comparison to other surveys.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

a constant-age population of galaxies is not a satisfactory explanation for the excess of blue galaxies in the counts, although the possibility that the excess is due to the formation of new galaxies at low red-shift cannot be excluded.

the faint blue counts are produced by a population of galaxies which is evolving in the sense that it is fading and reddening with time, with the star-formation rate cycling in a way that is not yet fully understood.

the excess blue counts cannot be explained by a population of galaxies whose star-formation rates have remained constant since z = 1, but that the counts can be explained if a population of young galaxies is formed at a constant rate since z ~ 1 and fades to a blue galaxy at z < 0 (Gronwall & Koo) or z < 0:3 (this paper).
The main takeaway from our work is that
the faint blue galaxy counts cannot be produced by a population of galaxies that is eternally young and has a star-formation history that is constant in time.

a constant-age population of star-forming galaxies, which is not inconsistent with the observed luminosity functions, is a poor fit to the deep galaxy counts, even when the selection criteria are taken into account.
the excess of faint galaxies is not a simple consequence of a passive population of galaxies with a fixed star formation rate.
